Um, starting with regular attendance, meaning that as a student that's present on a consistent basis, uh, if they're missing less than ten percent of the enrolled school days, um, missing less than ten percent of the enrolled school days during the school year. Um, chronic absenteeism is defined as really as, as, as a measurement of loss of instruction

time, um, when a student misses ten percent or more of the school year for, for any reason. So that, that includes excused absences, unexcused absences, and out-of-school suspensions. Uh, what it excludes is students enrolled less than fifty percent of the school year, uh, students receiving homebound instruction, in-school suspension, and alternative disciplinary placements. Uh, next slide, please. Um,

chronic absenteeism cr-- considerations. After viewing the data today, just looking at some of these considerations, take these into account. facing, um, such as chronic illnesses, lack of food or housing, mental health, or lack of access to mental health or healthcare. So on, on that, on that day, our chronic absenteeism rate was right at eleven percent. Um, when we pulled the, uh, the data today for our division-wide, chronic absenteeism rate is at twelve percent. Um, but we felt like it was important to help tell the story, to look at, at that-- the twenty-two/twenty-three school year.... So you see that at that year, our rate was at nineteen percent. Um, that was a significant year for

us in terms of attendance and how we, how we view attendance and now. Yeah, it really was. In terms of, you know, our, our strategies and how we, you know, what we're doing, um, to, uh, combat chronic absenteeism. Um, going in, we had to define, like, well, what is driving chronic absenteeism in our school division? Um, so at that, at that time, uh, Ms. Evans and myself, we were-- were tasked with the responsibility of creating a

chronic absenteeism work group. Uh, within that work group, we had principals at each level. We had our Dr. Tyler, Dr. Blalock, as part of, you know, our RASI team was present. Uh, we had attendance officers, uh, members from Unified Mental Health team. We wanted to get a lens from, uh, different perspectives and feedback on what we-- what, what are the target areas and what are some of the populations that we need to focus on to reduce our chronic absenteeism. Um, some of the actions that came out of that was, one, we need more

communication with our, with our communities, but particularly our, our EL and our Hispanic families. Uh, we, we developed a collaboration with our FACE office and are working hand in hand with our parent as educational partners to go out and do presentations to a lot of, to a lot of those communities of our Spa-- Hispanic families and providing, um, awareness and education and resources to those families. Uh, in addition to, um,

changing our policy or revisions to our policy and, and, and, um, our Regulation Eight one forty, we needed more guidelines on what is considered the criteria for an excused and, and unexcused absences. Um, w-- at the time, in that year, we also did not have a dedicated truancy docket with the juvenile court service unit. So we had several meetings with, uh, judges, our common attorney's office, um, uh, administration from our, our court

service unit to, to get our court, our docket back up and running, uh, for, for some of our most vulnerable students that are experiencing attendance gaps. Um, there are several other action steps that were taken. I, I think, you know, RASI was instrumental, um, giving a shout out to RASI now, to Dr. Tyler, Dr. Blalock, in really identifying, you know, like, that the profile for our chronically absent student in Loudoun County, which was really important, um, especially when it comes to educating our, our families

about the impacts of chronic absenteeism. Um, the result of that work was the following year that we, we were able to reduce our chronic absenteeism by five percent to... in, in that twenty-three, twenty-four year to fourteen percent, and we've been staying pretty steady at that rate, um, as well. Definitely. I just wanted to add that in doing our data dive, we, um, had some hypotheses that we would think that the students who were

chronically absent were students who were getting poor grades, who were having discipline referrals, or who were facing mental health challenges. And what we found was that that was not true. There are some small numbers of those students who did have those correlations, but the large number of students who were missing, were missing because of excused absences, so only a small percentage were the unexcused. So it was travel days, it was family trips, and that's what led us to changing our policy.
